title: Own Goal Dani
part: PART ONE: EIGHT GAMES, ZERO WINS

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #4: Kick the ball into your own net, then apologize to the ball.*

Sunday night, the video has four hundred views. I watched it eleven times. That is not a typo. Eleven is a specific number, like the players on a field, and I need to know exactly why it is funny. It is not funny. It is a disaster wearing a smile.

The clip starts with me running. Then I hit the ball. Then it goes in. The wrong net. The sound is muted, but someone added a sad trombone. A *waa-waa-waa* that lasts exactly as long as my face crumples.

Then comes the zoom.

The video creator, who goes by "HornetHunter99," slowed it down. He zoomed in tight on my face. I am holding the ball under my arm. I am looking at it. I am saying, "I'm sorry."

In the slow motion, my apology looks like a prayer. It looks like I am begging the leather sphere for forgiveness. It looks like I have no idea what I am doing.

I close my laptop. I open it again. I watch it a twelfth time. I need to see if there is an angle where I look cool. There is no angle where I look cool.
pages.image: A close-up of a laptop screen displaying a video of a girl in a yellow armband holding a soccer ball, with a sad trombone icon and a zoomed-in face expression, in a dimly lit bedroom.

pages.text:
Monday morning, the hallway at Harbor Valley Middle smells like floor wax mixed with the distinct, metallic scent of nervous sweat. I walk with my shoulders hiked up to my ears, trying to look like a statue, because statues do not get whooped by other students.

"Whoops!" a boy yells, doing the hand-over-shoulder motion without even looking at me. He does it to his friend.

Another kid leans in, grinning. "Need directions to the right net, Dani?"

I want to say something with teeth. I want to tell him my name is Dani Ruiz and that I have the fastest sprint time in the league. Instead, I say, "I think I am lost."

Carter Boyle is walking ahead of me. He turns, grinning. "It's just a joke, Ruiz. Chill out."

My best friend, Nia, bumps my shoulder. She is calm, and she is being kind. She hands me a juice box. "They don't mean anything, Dan. It's just a video."

I cannot stand it. I cannot stand her kindness. It feels like she is looking at a broken toy and saying, "Oh, you are okay, little thing." I am not a broken toy. I am a captain.
pages.image: A hallway scene where a girl in a yellow armband looks upset while a classmate gestures a "whoops" motion; a friend offers a juice box; a boy smiles in the background.

pages.text:
My room is quiet, except for the hum of the air conditioner and the heavy silence of the red notebook sitting on my bed. It is my Loss Log, and I keep it because if I do not write the failures down, they will eat me alive while I sleep.

I open it to the very back, where the pages are thin and white.

*Way to Lose #1: Show up.*
*Way to Lose #2: Let the ball hit your foot and go in.*
*Way to Lose #3: Be the best player and still lose.*

I stare at the list. I have never written a way we played well. I have never once jotted down "Great Pass" or "Good Tackle" or "Fast Run." In my head, a good game only counts if the scoreboard agrees. If the final number is 0 to 8, the good passes simply did not happen. The fast runs did not matter. The good tackles were just the exact moment before the bad goal.

I pick up my pen. My hand hovers over the paper, trembling slightly, trying to find a stable surface on the shaking desk. I try to write *Good Tackle* next to game eight, but the ink smudges instantly. It looks like a mistake. It looks like a lie.

I close the book. The red cover drops, hitting my chest with the dull, heavy thud of a wet towel.
pages.image: A red notebook lying open on a bed, with a pen hovering over a page of handwritten text; a girl's hand holds the pen, her face not visible.

pages.text:
Dinner is a loud place because my dad is doing his thing. He holds up the foam finger, the one with "GO" written in blue marker, and waves it at me like a conductor trying to get the orchestra to play louder.

"You are the best player out there, *mija*!" he announces. "You have the heart of a lion! The speed of a cheetah!"

"Dad," I say, staring at my plate. "We lost eight to zero."

"Details!" he waves his hand, dismissing the number as if it were a fly on the table. "The spirit is what matters!"

Abuela, who is eating her rice with the precision of a surgeon, looks up from her bowl. "She should have kicked the boy with the phone," she says. "In the shins. He was recording. That is a crime."

Luz, my little sister, slides a piece of paper across the table. It is a crayon drawing of a duck. The duck is wearing a yellow armband. It has a smile.

I look at the duck, then at Dad, then at Abuela. I laugh. It is a short, sharp laugh, like a balloon popping in a quiet room. Then I stop. The silence in my chest is louder than the television.
pages.image: A dinner table scene with a man waving a foam finger, a woman looking sharp-eyed, a young girl pushing a crayon drawing of a duck wearing an armband toward the center.

pages.text:
The email lands at 9:15 PM, right in the middle of my homework. It comes from the Harbor Valley League, and the subject line just says *Staffing Update*.

"Dear Parents, Mr. Dunphy has resigned his position to spend more time with his aquarium. We are looking for a new coach."

I stare at the screen until the letters blur. An aquarium. A man who wants to watch fish. We are the Mud Hens, not a decorative feature for a living room. We do not need a guy staring at bubbles; we need someone who understands that we are the bottom of the league by a wide margin.

I look down at my cleats. The laces are one green and one orange, tied tight and ready for a game that no longer feels worth playing.

I open the team chat. My fingers hover over the keyboard, trembling a little.

"I think maybe I am done," I type.

I read it back. It is the truth, but it is also a surrender, like waving a white flag in the wind. I do not send it. Not yet. I close the laptop with a sharp click, and the dark room suddenly feels like a closet.
pages.image: A pair of soccer cleats with green and orange laces sitting on a rug next to a closed laptop; the room is dark, with a single desk lamp casting a shadow.
